title: Agent Mesh: Reliability Primitives for Non-Idempotent Agent Delegation - Identity Adequacy and Evidence Adequacy
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 26 Aug 2026]
    Title:Agent Mesh: Reliability Primitives for Non-Idempotent Agent Delegation - Identity Adequacy and Evidence Adequacy
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Autonomous agents increasingly perform bounded software tasks under an orchestrator that retries, resumes, and budgets them. The machinery such orchestrators reach for is the service mesh's: retry, timeout, and error-rate circuit breaking. We report a failure study of a production agentic software-delivery platform over 147 numbered incidents spanning 81 runs, each with a measured cost and, in most cases, a mutation proof reproducing the failure. All three assumptions those primitives rest on are violated in practice, and we quantify the consequences: a loop of fifty-four consecutive successful tool calls no error-rate breaker could see; a progress signal constant by construction, guaranteeing a false trip on the third repair round and driving one run from six of six components to three; twenty-one events accumulated across six invocations of one delegation, making a correct, idempotent component unwinnable; a misrouted failure that woke five components for a two-component fault, leaving three bystanders regressing working code; and twelve incidents in which the enforcement layer blocked correct work, the most expensive costing 107 agent turns and zero accepted writes. We find one cross-cutting cause and its dual. Identity adequacy: in five separate subsystems an identity that failed to discriminate produced a confident wrong answer, and two of them derived the corrective rule independently. Evidence adequacy: a reliability decision may be taken only on evidence capable of moving, attributable to what it measures, and deterministic under identical conditions. From the findings we derive seven reliability primitives whose enforcement unit is the delegation rather than the message, and specify the controlled evaluation the study motivates but does not constitute.

report.summary: Study of production AI agents finds retries, timeouts, and circuit breakers fail due to identity and evidence inadequacy; proposes seven delegation-level reliability primitives.
report.background: As autonomous agents take on bounded software tasks, orchestrators increasingly rely on service-mesh style mechanisms: retry, timeout, and error-rate circuit breaking. These mechanisms assume messages are idempotent and that failures are visible at the message level. The authors analyzed a production agentic software-delivery platform, collecting 147 incidents across 81 runs, each with measured cost and mutation proof. They found all three assumptions violated in practice, causing cascading regressions, blocked correct work, and false circuit trips. The study identifies two root causes: identity adequacy, where identities fail to distinguish important differences and lead to confident wrong answers, and evidence adequacy, where reliability decisions use evidence that cannot move, is not attributable, or is nondeterministic. The paper derives seven reliability primitives enforced at the delegation level, not the message level, and calls for controlled evaluation.
key_points: Service-mesh reliability tooling is unsafe for agent orchestration: retries, timeouts, and error-rate circuit breakers all assume failures behave like simple network calls, but the study found a loop of 54 successful tool calls invisible to error-rate breakers and a constant progress signal that guaranteed a false trip on the third repair round.

Identity adequacy matters: in five separate subsystems, an identity that failed to discriminate produced confident wrong answers. Two of these subsystems independently derived the same incorrect corrective rule, showing the problem is structural, not just an isolated bug in one component.

Evidence adequacy is the second root cause: reliability decisions require evidence that can actually move, is attributable to what it measures, and is deterministic under identical conditions. The paper shows how 21 accumulated events across six invocations made a correct, idempotent component unwinnable.

Reliability enforcement can actively block correct work: twelve incidents involved the enforcement layer preventing valid operations, with the most expensive costing 107 agent turns and zero accepted writes. This means naive guardrails can be more harmful than the failures they try to prevent.

The proposed answer is shifting enforcement from messages to delegations, using seven reliability primitives. This re-centers system design around the complete unit of work being delegated, rather than individual tool calls, and demands controlled studies to validate the approach.
report.impact: This paper signals that agentic systems cannot simply adopt decades-old microservice reliability patterns. For developers, it means orchestrators must treat delegation as a first-class reliability boundary, with richer identity semantics and evidence telemetry for every decision. For the AI industry, it pushes frameworks toward inspection, deterministic replay, and per-delegation budgets rather than message-level stats. For regular users, it suggests that while agents become more capable, their failure modes will become more surprising unless reliability contracts mature; a small misidentification can cascade into regressions across unrelated components. The study also implies that evaluation and observability standards must evolve alongside agent capabilities to avoid confidence in systems that are actively, invisibly failing.
report.tools: To explore these concepts, watch orchestration frameworks that expose delegation control, such as LangGraph and Temporal for durable workflow semantics. OpenTelemetry can provide evidence-grade trace and metric telemetry, while OPA (Open Policy Agent) supports policy enforcement at the delegation boundary. Service-mesh projects like Istio and Linkerd are useful to contrast the message-level primitives the paper critiques.
